title: Chapter L

teacherSummary.text: Elizabeth realizes Darcy is the man who would have suited her best, just as she believes the family disgrace has ended her chances. Wickham is to join the regulars in the north.

vocabulary.context: An union of a different tendency, and precluding the possibility of the other, was soon to be formed in their family.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “preclude”: pre- (Latin prae, "before"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To run away, or escape privately, from the place or station to which one is bound by duty
vocabulary.context: She was more alive to the disgrace, which the want of new clothes must reflect on her daughter’s nuptials, than to any sense of shame at her eloping and living with Wickham, a fortnight before they took place.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “elope”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.context: Wickham’s intention to go into the regulars; and, among his former friends, there are still some who are able and willing to assist him in the army.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “regular”: re- (Latin re-, "back, again"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To add after something else has been said or written
vocabulary.context: And will you give yourself the trouble of carrying similar assurances to his creditors in Meryton, of whom I shall subjoin a list, according to his information.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “subjoin”: sub- (Latin sub, "under"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: A thin cotton, white, dyed, or printed
vocabulary.context: The marriage of a daughter, which had been the first object of her wishes since Jane was sixteen, was now on the point of accomplishment, and her thoughts and her words ran wholly on those attendants of elegant nuptials, fine muslins, new carriages, and servants.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “muslin”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: Performing, or ready to perform, the duties required by one who has the right to claim submission, obedience, or…
vocabulary.context: She is well, and begs to be dutifully remembered to you and her mother.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “dutiful”: -ful (Old English -full, "full of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To drive back or away, as with the foot
vocabulary.context: What a triumph for him, as she often thought, could he know that the proposals which she had proudly spurned only four months ago, would now have been gladly and gratefully received!
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “spurn”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.context: Not, however, from any fear of disadvantage from it, individually to herself; for at any rate, there seemed a gulf impassable between them.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “impassable”: im- (Latin in-, "not" or "in") + pass (Latin passus, "step") + -able (Latin -abilis, "able to be"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: To shut up apart from others
vocabulary.context: To be sure it would have been more for the advantage of conversation, had Miss Lydia Bennet come upon the town; or, as the happiest alternative, been secluded from the world, in some distant farm house.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “seclude”: se- (Latin se-, "apart"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: Darcy would connect himself with a family, where to every other objection would now be added, an alliance and relationship of the nearest kind with the man whom he so justly scorned.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “scorn”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

context.history: Austen often places realization at the point where hope seems lost.

significance: Elizabeth's longing reflects her full change of heart.
discussionQuestions: Why does Elizabeth recognize her love only now?
Where does characterization appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with women's limited choices?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter L,” how does Austen show too late? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Chapter L, how does Austen develop the idea of too late? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the characterization in the chapter helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter L develops the idea of too late. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and theme shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Chapter L (where it begins, turns and ends) and its characterization shape the reader's understanding of too late. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Chapter L suggests about too late. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the chapter's characterization and theme), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses characterization in Chapter L to complicate the reader's understanding of too late. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter L within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of too late responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Chapter L alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the chapter's handling of too late follows or bends those conventions, using the characterization as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Chapter L and its treatment of too late. State your method, show what it reveals in the chapter's characterization and theme, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Chapter L as evidence for a larger claim about too late in Pride and Prejudice. Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter L as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of too late. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

satQuestions.passage: Wickham’s intention to go into the regulars; and, among his former friends, there are still some who are able and willing to assist him in the army.
satQuestions.prompt: As used in the text, what does the word “regulars” most nearly mean?
options: To shut up apart from others

satQuestions.passage: The good news quickly spread through the house; and with proportionate speed through the neighbourhood. It was borne in the latter with decent philosophy. To be sure it would have been more for the advantage of conversation, had Miss Lydia Bennet come upon the town; or, as the happiest alternative, been secluded from the world, in some distant farm house. But there was much to be talked of, in marrying her; and the good-natured wishes for her well-doing, which had proceeded before, from all the spiteful old ladies in Meryton, lost but little of their spirit in this change of circumstances, because with such a husband, her misery was considered certain.
satQuestions.prompt: Which choice best states a central concern of “Chapter L”?

annotationFocus.label: Characterization
annotationFocus.lookFor: what characters say, do and think, and how others react to them
annotationFocus.passage: The good news quickly spread through the house; and with proportionate speed through the neighbourhood. It was borne in the latter with decent philosophy. To be sure it would have been more for the advantage of conversation, had Miss Lydia Bennet come upon the town; or, as the happiest alternative, been secluded from the world, in some distant farm house. But there was much to be talked of, in marrying her; and the good-natured wishes for her well-doing, which had proceeded before, from all the spiteful old ladies in Meryton, lost but little of their spirit in this change of circumstances, because with such a husband, her misery was considered certain.

annotationFocus.label: Theme
annotationFocus.lookFor: statements or moments that connect to the book's big ideas

annotationFocus.label: Irony
annotationFocus.lookFor: gaps between what characters expect or say and what is true

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Why does Elizabeth recognize her love only now? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are precluding, eloping, regulars, subjoin, muslins. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “An union of a different tendency, and precluding the possibility of the other, was soon to be formed in their family.” Webster's says: To put a barrier before. Now the word history: “preclude”: pre- (Latin prae, "before"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “elope”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin. “regular”: re- (Latin re-, "back, again"). Root not in our table: have students find it. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. Austen often places realization at the point where hope seems lost. Why does this chapter matter? Elizabeth's longing reflects her full change of heart. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for characterization.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see characterization, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to too late.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Characterization, Theme, Irony.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of characterization. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: The good news quickly spread through the house; and with proportionate speed through the neighbourhood. It was borne in the latter with decent philosophy. To be sure it would have been more for the advantage of conversation, had Miss Lydia Bennet come upon the town; or, as the happiest alternative, been secluded from the world, in some distant farm house. But there was much to be talked of, in marrying her; and the good-natured wishes for her well-doing, which had proceeded before, from all the spiteful old ladies in Meryton, lost but little of their spirit in this change of circumstances, because with such a husband, her misery was considered certain.

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their rigor.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Characterization, Theme, Irony: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Chapter L,” how does Austen show too late? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to first impressions and prejudice? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about too late, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how characterization shapes too late. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
